q-49614.worked_solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =4x+1 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =4 \\ \text{d}u & =4\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u & =\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=4x+1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 2 \\ u & 1 & 9\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{{(4x+1)}^{3}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{9}{u}^{3/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {\frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}|}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{2}{5}({9}^{5/2}-{1}^{5/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}(({3}^{2})^{5/2}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}({3}^{5}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}(243-1) \\  & =\frac{242}{10} \\  & =\frac{121}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-49527.name: Question 2
q-49527.worked_solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =2x-1 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2 \\ \text{d}u & =2\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u & =\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=2x-1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 1 & 2 \\ u & 1 & 3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{2x-1}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{3}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}({3}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(({3}^{3})^{1/2}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(3\sqrt{3}-1) \\  & =\sqrt{3}-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-17102.name: Question 5
q-17102.worked_solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =3x+1 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =3 \\ \text{d}u & =3\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u & =\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=3x+1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 1 \\ u & 1 & 4\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{(3x+1)}^{3}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{4}{u}^{3/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {\frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{2}{5}({4}^{5/2}-{1}^{5/2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{15}(({2}^{2})^{5/2}-1) \\  & =\frac{2}{15}({2}^{5}-1) \\  & =\frac{2}{15}(32-1) \\  & =\frac{62}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-73432.name: Question 6
q-73432.worked_solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & ={x}^{4}+9 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =4{x}^{3} \\ \text{d}u & =4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u & ={x}^{3}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u={x}^{4}+9.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 2 \\ u & 9 & 25\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{({x}^{4}+9)}\,{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{9}^{25}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{9}^{25}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{9}^{25}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(u){|}_{9}^{25} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(25)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot 2(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{5}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

q-73434.name: Question 7
q-73434.worked_solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & ={x}^{3}+2 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2} \\ \text{d}u & =3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u & ={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u={x}^{3}+2.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & -1 & 1 \\ u & 1 & 3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{1}{({x}^{3}+2)}\,{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(u){|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =2{x}^{3}+4 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2} \\ \text{d}u & =6{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u & =3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 1 & 2 \\ u & 6 & 20\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{2{x}^{3}+4}\cdot 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{6}^{20}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u.
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & ={x}^{2}+1 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x \\ \text{d}u & =2x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u & =x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & \sqrt{3} \\ u & 1 & 4\end{aligned}
$$

So, the first integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{({x}^{2}+1)}\,x\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.

To evaluate the second integral, we can use the definition of $\operatorname{arctan}⁡x.$ Finally, we can solve the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u+{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u+\operatorname{arctan}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(u){|}_{1}^{4}+(\frac{\pi }{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1))+\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{2})+\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
